nameStory: The 'narrow triangle' in this moonwort's name comes from the distinctive triangular shape of its fertile frond segments, which are notably slender compared to other moonworts. Like all moonworts, it gets the 'moon' part of its name from the crescent-shaped sporangia (spore cases) that release spores in late summer, resembling tiny moons scattered along the frond.
description: Narrow triangle moonwort is a tiny, delicate fern that's easy to overlook in the forest. This diminutive plant typically stands just 2-6 inches tall and consists of a single sterile frond (the leafy part) and a separate fertile frond (the spore-bearing stalk). The sterile frond is divided into narrow, triangular segments that give the plant its name, while the fertile frond rises above it like a tiny candelabra. Unlike typical ferns, moonworts don't unfurl from fiddleheads but emerge already formed in early summer.

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Single sterile frond divided into narrow, triangular segments that feel thin and papery to the touch, typically with 3-7 pairs of segments arranged along the main stem

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Extremely small plant, usually 2-6 inches tall total, with the fertile spore-bearing stalk typically taller than the leafy sterile frond

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Tiny round sporangia clustered on branched stalks above the sterile frond, turning from green to golden-brown when mature and feeling slightly gritty when touched

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: Smooth, fleshy stem that's often pinkish or reddish at the base, feeling succulent rather than wiry like most fern stems

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Nearly always found in rich, moist soil among mosses and leaf litter in shaded areas, often hidden beneath taller plants

habitat: This rare moonwort grows in rich, moist soils of mature hardwood and mixed forests, particularly in areas with maples, birches, and hemlocks. Look for it in shaded spots with deep leaf litter and mossy ground, often on gentle slopes or in small forest clearings. It seems to prefer slightly acidic soils and is most often found at mid-elevations in mountainous areas of New England.

seasonality.spring: Plants begin emerging from underground in late spring, but are still very small and easily missed among emerging wildflowers and unfurling ferns.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when both sterile and fertile fronds are fully developed, with spores maturing from green to golden-brown by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Fronds begin yellowing and withering as spores are released, becoming increasingly difficult to spot among fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, spending the season as an underground gametophyte and root system.

funFact: Moonworts have one of the most unusual life cycles in the plant world - they can spend 10-15 years growing underground as a tiny, colorless gametophyte before ever producing their first visible frond, making them some of nature's most patient plants!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small moonworts, especially little grapefern, but narrow triangle moonwort's segments are distinctly more triangular and narrow rather than rounded or spoon-shaped. Memory trick: 'Narrow triangles' - if you can't see clear triangular shapes in the frond segments, it's probably a different moonwort species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'moonwort,' this plant is actually a fern, not an herb - the common name comes from medieval times when people thought the crescent-shaped sporangia had magical lunar properties. The extreme rarity of observations (only 69 recorded in all of New England) makes this one of our region's most elusive native plants.
compareHints: Narrow triangle moonwort differs from matricary grapefern by having much narrower, more pointed segments rather than finely dissected, lacy ones. Unlike little grapefern, its segments are clearly triangular rather than rounded or oval. Compared to other moonworts in the region, it's generally smaller overall and has the most distinctly angular segment shape.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Matricary grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its chamomile-like leaf segments that are more finely divided than most of its relatives.
**[Uncertain claim flagged: specific comparison details]** Swamp moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for wet habitats and its small, fan-shaped sterile frond segments.
Little grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its simple, often undivided leaf blade, whereas matricary grapefern and others have multiple leaflets or more complex divisions.

Upswept moonwort differs from other moonworts by its fan or wedge-shaped leaflet segments that angle upward, rather than the more rounded or deeply divided segments of relatives like matricary grapefern.
Unlike its moonwort relatives with their more typical triangular or oval leaflet shapes, spathulate moonwort's spatula-shaped segments are unmistakable.
Prairie moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for dry, prairie-like conditions rather than the moist, shaded habitats preferred by most of its relatives.
